THE MOLECULE BEHIND THE MESSAGE

A little introduction to DNA.

A ↔ TC ↔ G

DNA is a double helix. Its bases pair A with T and C with G. The order of these letters carries genetic information.

DNA→mRNA→Amino acids

Transcription copies information into RNA. Translation reads mRNA codons to build an amino acid chain.

✳

A mutation is a change in DNA. It is not automatically a disease.

KEEP THIS IN MIND

LIVE COMPARISON

ABOUT THIS MODEL

This invented 18-base sequence is not a human gene. It uses the standard genetic code and a fixed reading frame to teach single-base substitutions. It does not model splicing, gene regulation, protein folding, or a person’s cancer risk.

A → G

Same amino acid

FROM CLASS

A synonymous substitution changes a codon without changing its amino acid. “Same protein sequence” does not guarantee no biological effect in every real gene.

Glu → Val

Different amino acid

FROM CLASS

A missense substitution changes an amino acid. The effect depends on where it happens and what that protein does.

Trp → STOP

An earlier ending

SMALL EXTENSION

A nonsense substitution introduces an early stop codon. The message may make a shorter protein, or the cell may break down the RNA.

02 / FROM MESSAGES TO CELL BEHAVIOR

Growth needs
checks and balances.

Some genes help cells grow. Others help control division or repair DNA damage. Cancer can develop as multiple safeguards are disrupted.

Class #6 · PDF pp. 20–26

EXPLORE THE SAFEGUARDS

CONCEPTUAL CELL CULTURE

A separate qualitative illustration—not a simulation of the DNA sequence above. Cell spacing and appearance are symbolic; they do not predict cancer, growth rates, or probabilities.

↗

More than one genetic change is generally involved in cancer. An inherited risk variant increases risk; it does not make cancer certain.

03 / MAKING THE CONNECTION

From code to cells.

In computer science, changing one character can change what a program does. In biology, changing one DNA base can change a message—but context matters.

This project uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to make an invisible process easier to explore. Comparing the same input and output helps us ask a better question: what changed, and what evidence do we need before drawing a conclusion?

The coding analogy has limits: cells are living systems with repair, regulation, and many interacting molecules.
